inputs.need:
I am the nursing research lead at a 520-bed acute hospital with 18 adult inpatient units. Our nurses keep telling us that care is left undone on busy shifts: mouth care, turning, walking patients, talking with patients before discharge, and sometimes timed medicines. The chief nursing officer wants numbers before the next budget round, and our nurses' union wants the same numbers for a different argument, so the method has to be something both sides will trust.

We plan a cross-sectional survey of registered nurses and licensed practical nurses on all 18 units in one four-week window this winter, using a missed-care checklist that asks each nurse about their last shift. We also have the scheduling system, which holds planned and actual nurse hours per unit and shift, and the patient acuity scores that charge nurses enter each morning. I would like to link each response to the staffing of the unit on the shift the nurse describes, so we can see whether missed care goes up when a unit runs below its planned staffing, and whether that holds after acuity is taken into account.

I need help choosing and adapting the checklist, working out how many responses we need and what response rate is realistic, deciding what 'short-staffed' means (patients per nurse, hours per patient day, or planned versus actual hours), and handling the fact that nurses on the same unit and shift are not independent. Two things worry me: some of what I have read says staffing explains most missed care and some says it disappears once acuity is included, and I do not know how to stop the results being used to blame individual nurses.
inputs.constraints: The survey must close by 2027-02-28. No incentive budget; completion is allowed during 20 minutes of paid time. Results are reported by unit and never by individual nurse.

About 1,150 registered and licensed practical nurses work on the 18 adult inpatient units.

response.title: Missed nursing care and shift-level staffing on 18 adult inpatient units
response.subtitle: Cross-sectional last-shift survey linked to unit staffing and acuity
response.statement: Nurses report that care is left undone on busy shifts, but the hospital has no measure of how often, of which activities, or whether missed care rises when a unit runs below planned staffing once patient acuity is considered. Management and the union both want figures they can trust. A last-shift survey of nurses linked to the scheduling and acuity records of the shift each nurse describes would answer this at one point in time.
response.whoAffected: Adult inpatients on 18 units, especially dependent older patients who need turning, mouth care and help to walk; about 1,150 registered and licensed practical nurses; unit managers and the budget committee.
response.whatHurts: Missed turning and mobilisation lead to pressure injuries and deconditioning, missed teaching leaves patients unprepared for discharge, and late timed medicines can cause harm. Nurses describe moral distress when they cannot finish care.
response.currentPractice: No routine measure of missed care. Staffing is planned by a core schedule and adjusted daily; acuity scores are entered each morning but not linked to any outcome.
response.whyNow: The next budget round, conflicting claims from management and the union, and an REB approval and union agreement already in place.
response.patientCenteredGoal: Patients on every unit receive essential nursing care on every shift, and staffing decisions rest on evidence that nurses and managers both accept.
response.summary: Problem framed as a cross-sectional survey question on missed care and shift-level staffing, with acuity as the key competing explanation.

records.title: Nurse staffing and missed nursing care in 32 hospitals: a cross-sectional survey of registered nurses
records.authors: Oyelaran-Strand P, Kowalczyk-Ade M, Haddad-Lindgren S
records.abstract: We surveyed 1,410 registered nurses on medical and surgical units in 32 hospitals using a 22-item missed-care checklist about the last shift worked. At least one activity was left undone on the last shift by 71 percent of nurses, most often comfort talk, mouth care and patient teaching. Each additional patient per registered nurse was associated with higher odds of reporting missed care (odds ratio 1.09, 95 percent CI 1.04 to 1.14). Units with more licensed practical nurses in the skill mix reported more missed teaching and discharge preparation. Staffing was reported by the nurses themselves, and the response rate was 38 percent.

records.title: Missed care on medical and surgical wards: results of a union-led member survey
records.abstract: An online survey of 2,960 members working on medical and surgical wards asked about care left undone on the most recent shift. Sixty-eight percent reported at least one missed activity, and 41 percent reported a missed or late timed medicine. Respondents described short staffing, unplanned admissions and sick calls as the main reasons. The report gives no response rate and no information on how the survey was distributed, and its publication date is not stated anywhere in the document. Free-text comments describe night shifts as the hardest to cover.

records.title: Shift-level staffing shortfalls and missed care: linking nurse reports to scheduling records
records.authors: Brandt-Achebe L, Morales-Okoro J, Svensson-Iqbal R
records.abstract: Nurses on 12 units reported missed care at the end of 2,870 shifts over six months, and each report was linked to planned and actual nursing hours from the scheduling system. Missed care was reported after 44 percent of shifts that ran at least 10 percent below planned hours and after 27 percent of shifts at or above plan. The difference persisted after adjustment for the unit's mean acuity score. Night shifts had fewer reports overall but a steeper increase with shortfall. Linking reports to the actual shift avoided relying on nurses' recall of their staffing.

records.title: Instruments for measuring missed nursing care: a systematic review of measurement properties
records.authors: Nakamura-Fitch E, Obi-Castellanos R, Petit-Wanjiru D
records.abstract: We identified 14 instruments that measure missed or unfinished nursing care. Internal consistency was reported for 12 and test-retest reliability for 5. Construct validity was supported for 6 instruments, mostly by correlations with staffing. Instruments differed in recall period, from the last shift to the last month, and in whether they asked about the reasons for missed care. A last-shift recall period and a separate reasons section were recommended to reduce recall bias and to separate what was missed from why. None of the instruments had been validated for licensed practical nurses.

records.title: Patient acuity, staffing and missed care: accounting for acuity weakens the association
records.abstract: In this conference abstract, 640 nurses on 20 units reported missed care for their last shift, and unit staffing was measured as patients per nurse. Unadjusted, each additional patient per nurse was associated with more missed care (odds ratio 1.11). After adjustment for the mean acuity score of the unit on the survey day, the association was no longer clear (odds ratio 1.03, 95 percent CI 0.97 to 1.10). The authors suggest that staffing ratios already reflect acuity in units that staff to acuity. Methods are described briefly and the year of the meeting is not given.

records.title: Improving response to hospital nurse surveys: protected time versus reminders
records.venue: Survey Methods in Health Workforce Research
records.abstract: Across 16 units in two hospitals, we compared a web survey with three email reminders against the same survey completed during 20 minutes of protected paid time. Response was 31 percent with reminders and 52 percent with protected time. Responders under reminders were more often day-shift and full-time nurses, whereas protected time narrowed the difference between day and night shifts. Item nonresponse was similar in both arms. Protected time cost about 9 nursing hours per 100 responses, which the hospitals judged affordable for an annual survey.

records.title: Missed nursing care and patient-reported experience on medical units
records.authors: Achebe-Sorensen F, Varga-Tanaka I, Reid-Mensah O
records.abstract: We matched unit-level missed care rates from a nurse survey with patient experience scores from 3,400 discharged patients on 26 medical units. Units where nurses more often reported missed comfort talk and teaching had lower patient ratings of being told about new medicines and of help with pain. The association with overall ratings was weak. Patient experience surveys were returned by 29 percent of discharged patients, so the matched units differ in who answered. Unit-level aggregation cannot show which patients received less care.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level; two undated grey records are left unrated. Surveys consistently find that most nurses leave at least one activity undone on the last shift. Two dated studies link higher workload or below-plan shifts to more missed care (odds ratio 1.09 per patient; 44 against 27 percent of shifts), and the shift-level study kept its association after acuity adjustment, while an undated conference abstract found it unclear after adjustment. Protected time roughly doubles response. No instrument is validated for licensed practical nurses. The evidence supports a last-shift survey linked to shift staffing with acuity measured, and does not settle how much acuity explains.
response.gradeRationale: Cross-sectional self-report designs with modest response, one conflicting unappraisable abstract, and indirect patient outcomes; consistent direction for the staffing association but serious risk of bias.
response.summary: Seven records appraised; two undated records left unrated; five claims including one conflicting claim with high uncertainty.

steps.note: The annotations for the two undated records omit relevance, methodQuality and grade, so they stay null and 'unrated' (G4): an omitted score is never filled with a default. Claim c2 rests on an undated, unrated record and carries high uncertainty. Applying annotations and claims requires S13.

response.reading: Missed care is the end of a chain that starts with planned staffing, is bent by sick calls and unplanned admissions on the day, and is loaded by patient acuity. Acuity is both a cause of missed care and, where units staff to acuity, a cause of staffing, which is why one abstract loses the association after adjustment and a shift-level study keeps it. The survey measures the nurse's own shift, so linking it to the actual hours of that shift avoids recall of staffing. Licensed practical nurses and night staff are the groups most likely to be under-represented or mismeasured.

response.rationale: The question is the prevalence of missed care and its association with the staffing of the shift described, at one point in time: a cross-sectional survey with linkage to scheduling and acuity records measures exactly that. The conflict between c2 and c3 is addressed by measuring acuity for the same shift rather than as a unit average. Reporting follows STROBE for cross-sectional studies.
alternatives: Repeated monthly survey panel (refused: the budget question needs one snapshot, and repeated surveys fatigue staff)
Direct observation of care (refused: costly, reactive and impossible across 18 units in four weeks)
Survey without scheduling linkage (refused: relies on nurses' recall of staffing)
response.whyNotMoreComplex: A longitudinal design would add little to a budget decision and would need repeated paid time the union has not agreed.

decision.statement: Run the last-shift cross-sectional survey on all 18 units in a four-week winter window during paid time, linking each response to the planned and actual hours and the acuity of the shift described, because shift shortfalls have been linked to missed care (c1, c3), protected time makes a usable response rate realistic (c4), and the checklist needs a pretest with licensed practical nurses (c5).
decision.question: Should the hospital run a last-shift missed care survey linked to shift staffing and acuity this winter?

criteria.text: Below-plan shifts have been associated with more missed care in linked or multi-hospital data.
Acuity fully explains the staffing association where units staff to acuity.

response.overview: Cross-sectional last-shift survey of registered and licensed practical nurses on 18 adult inpatient units over four weeks in January and February 2027, completed during 20 minutes of paid time, with each response linked to the planned and actual hours and the acuity of the unit on the shift described.
response.population: All registered and licensed practical nurses who worked at least one shift on one of the 18 units in the survey window; agency staff excluded because they cannot be given paid time.
response.exposure: Shift staffing ratio: actual divided by planned nursing hours for the unit and shift described, from the scheduling system; below plan means at least 10 percent below. Patients per nurse on that shift is a secondary exposure.
response.procedures: The checklist is adapted from a 22-item last-shift instrument and pretested with eight licensed practical nurses and four registered nurses. Nurses complete it on a tablet during paid time on any shift, naming the unit, date and shift type of their last shift. The analyst links each response to the scheduling system and to the mean morning acuity score of that unit on that date, then deletes the date, keeping only the linked variables.

outcomes.measure: Count of the 22 activities reported as missed
outcomes.why: Shows the amount as well as the presence of missed care.

parsimony.simplestPath: One survey window, one primary outcome, one staffing exposure, one acuity adjustment.

response.theoreticalFramework: No framework beyond the survey design; SEIPS is used only to name work-system factors in the reasons section.
response.summary: Four-week linked last-shift survey with one primary outcome and response tracked by role and shift.

response.designSummary: Cross-sectional survey with shift-level linkage; prevalence of any missed care and its association with below-plan staffing, adjusted for acuity, with nurses clustered in units.
response.sampleSize: About 1,150 eligible nurses and a planned response near 50 percent with paid time (c4) give about 575 responses. For overall prevalence near 65 percent with a unit-level design effect of about 2.5, the 95 percent confidence interval is about 6 percentage points either side. For the primary association, about 30 percent of described shifts are expected to be below plan; because the exposure varies within units, the design effect is about 1.3, and 575 responses give about 80 percent power at two-sided alpha 0.05 for a 15-point difference (62 against 47 percent). Smaller differences would be estimated with wide intervals.
response.primaryAnalysis: Mixed-effects logistic regression of any missed care on below-plan shift, with a random intercept for unit, adjusted for acuity, shift type, role, unit type and years of experience; the unadjusted estimate is reported alongside.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Negative binomial model for the number of activities missed; the same model for missed timed medicines; item-level prevalence by role and shift type, descriptive only.
response.missingData: Responses without a usable last-shift date cannot be linked and are described separately; item nonresponse above 10 percent is handled by multiple imputation with 20 imputations.
response.multiplicity: One primary association; secondary outcomes and item-level results are labelled as secondary with confidence intervals only.
response.software: R with the lme4 package; the analysis plan is lodged with the steering group before the survey opens.
overfittingGuards: No data-driven cut-off for below plan
Cells under five responses suppressed, not merged after looking at results
response.summary: About 575 responses; about 80 percent power for a 15-point difference after a within-unit design effect of 1.3.

response.risks: Minimal: a 20-minute survey. The main risks are re-identification of nurses on small units or night shifts and use of the results against individuals.
response.consent: An information sheet on the tablet explains the purpose, the linkage to shift staffing and the reporting rule; completion implies consent, and nurses may skip any item or stop.
response.data: Responses are held by the research office, not by managers; after linkage the shift date is deleted; cells with fewer than five responses are suppressed in every report.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: licensed practical nurses, night and part-time staff and internationally educated nurses may be under-represented or misunderstood by an instrument not validated for them. Paid time is offered on every shift, the checklist is pretested with licensed practical nurses, and response is reported by role and shift. For patients, dependent older adults and people with limited English are most affected by missed talk and teaching.
response.effectiveness: Informs the budget round with a measure both sides accept; a null association after acuity adjustment is equally informative.
response.efficiency: About 190 paid nursing hours and existing extracts.
response.costs: Paid survey time under the union agreement; analyst time within existing roles.
response.partnerships: A joint steering group of two union representatives, two unit managers and two patient partners agrees the checklist wording and the reporting rule.
response.rebPath: Approved by the hospital REB as minimal risk (REB-26-1182); ICH-GCP and Declaration of Helsinki principles for confidentiality apply.
response.limitations: Self-report of missed care; acuity as a unit mean; one hospital; winter only.
response.summary: Minimal-risk survey under REB approval with a non-blaming reporting rule agreed with the union and management.

response.partnershipPlan: The joint steering group meets before fielding and after analysis; two patient partners review the plain-language summary.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; the union's anonymised member comments from last winter are read for themes.

items.implication: Keep turning and mobilisation as separate items and report them by shift type.

response.title: Missed nursing care and shift-level staffing shortfalls on adult inpatient units: a cross-sectional survey linked to scheduling records
response.abstract: Objective: to estimate the prevalence of missed nursing care and its association with below-plan staffing of the shift described, adjusted for acuity. Design: cross-sectional last-shift survey of registered and licensed practical nurses on 18 units, linked to scheduling and acuity records. Primary outcome: any of 22 activities missed on the last shift. Results and conclusions will be written after analysis.
response.introduction: Nurses report that care is left undone when shifts are short, but published studies disagree on whether acuity explains the association, and most rely on nurses' recall of their staffing. This study links each report to the recorded hours and acuity of the shift described.
response.methods: All eligible nurses were invited to complete a pretested 22-item checklist during paid time. Each response was linked to actual and planned hours and to unit acuity on the shift described. A mixed-effects logistic model with a unit random intercept estimated the association.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present response by role and shift, item-level prevalence, and unadjusted and acuity-adjusted associations.
response.discussion: The discussion will compare the findings with the retrieved shift-level and multi-hospital studies and with the undated conflicting abstract. It will set out what the figures mean for the budget round without attributing missed care to individual nurses.
response.limitations: Missed care is self-reported and acuity is a unit mean for the day. The study covers one hospital in one winter, and the instrument is not validated for licensed practical nurses.
response.conclusion: To be written after analysis. It will describe associations and will not attribute missed care to individual nurses.
response.summary: STROBE-structured draft; results left empty until the survey closes.
